memoryText: But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Isaiah 53:5 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This is the heart of the Old Testament’s picture of the cross. It was written some seven centuries before Jesus was born, and it describes what he would do in language that is hard to read without wonder.

“But he was pierced for our transgressions.” The word “pierced” means run through, wounded to the point of death. The Servant’s wounds are connected to something: our transgressions. The sin was ours. The piercing was his. “He was crushed for our iniquities.” The word “crushed” is the strongest word for breaking something to pieces. Iniquity is twisted behavior. Each phrase is a transfer. What belonged to us was borne by him.

“Upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace.” Chastisement is discipline, the punishment that was due. It fell on him, and the result is peace for us. Think about what this peace is: not just a feeling of calm, but reconciliation with God. The war between a holy God and a rebellious people has ended.

“And with his wounds we are healed.” The healing is the forgiveness of sins and the restoration of the whole person. 1 Peter 2:24 says that “by his wounds you have been healed.” The wounds that made him unrecognizable are the means of our wholeness. The scars of Christ are the glory of the gospel.

This verse can be said at any time. When you feel guilt, say it. When you are tempted to believe that you must earn God’s favor, say it. When you meet someone who has no hope, tell them. The Servant was wounded for us, and the debt is paid.
weekInReview: This week you walked through the center of Isaiah. You saw the idols of Babylon carried off on animals, while the true God carries his people from birth to old age. You heard the Servant speak, call him to be a light for the nations, and learned that God has engraved his people on the palms of his hands. Then you came to the heart of the book: the Servant who gave his back to those who strike, who was despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions, and crushed for our iniquities. On Wednesday’s doctrinal pause you traced the doctrine of the atonement through sacrifice, substitution, propitiation, redemption, and victory. After the cross came the invitation of Isaiah 55, “Come, everyone who thirsts.” And you prayed Psalms 22 and 69, in which the suffering Messiah speaks for himself. The week taught that Jesus bore our sins, that God is both just and the justifier, and that the invitation is free.
reflectionQuestions: Isaiah 53 says the Servant was pierced for our transgressions. What does it mean to you personally that Jesus took your place?
The doctrinal pause described the atonement through several pictures. Which one speaks most clearly to your own need right now: sacrifice, substitution, ransom, or victory?
Isaiah 55 invites everyone who thirsts to come without money. What would it mean for you to accept this invitation without trying to earn it?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he was pierced and crushed for you.
Thank him that by his wounds you are healed.
Rest in the peace he bought.
